chat.author: Benjamin Schwartz
chat.text: To be clear: TTL stretching as proposed here _does_ create enormous headaches for server operators.  It doesn't cause visible breakage because the operators have absorbed the cost, but is not trivial.

chat.author: Benjamin Schwartz
chat.text: We routinely try to turn something off, and are delayed by hours while we watch a graph of clients who are using it long after they should have migrated off, because of TTL stretching.

chat.author: Erik Nygren
chat.text:
The degree of stretching here also makes a big difference here and not all is the same.
For example what mDNSresponder does seems entirely reasonable to me:

The mDNSResponder code stretches TTLs by 25%, plus two seconds to account for minor clock variations. 

Something like that seems entirely reasonable to do in DNSOP.
That is very distinct from "try a few hours or days later" which is where the operational issues come in.

I'd think that you'd need to have to batch up responses to build a ladder around, but then the proof for the ladder might be queried against a completely different authority than the one which built the ladder.

chat.author: Benjamin Schwartz
chat.text: @Erik: Batch queries on each auth host in 100 microsecond increments.  Sign each batch with one signature.

chat.author: Ondřej Surý
chat.text: Ben, how does that help when the client (the attacker) control the queries?

chat.author: Benjamin Schwartz
chat.text: Ondrej: Send as many queries as you want.  The signer performs a constant number of signatures per second independent of QPS.

chat.author: Ondřej Surý
chat.text:
But you still want to answer legitimate queries at the same time.
And the Merkle trees are per-zone, so you can't batch them together.
This works for a large zone, but not for a large DNS hosting (like Cloudflare).

chat.author: Peter Thomassen
chat.text: just put all hosted zones in a Merkle tree :stuck_out_tongue_wink:

chat.author: Ondřej Surý
chat.text: That's probably where we are talking past each other :). The online signing works for large-zones where you can actually batch the RRsets to be signed.

chat.author: Ondřej Surý
chat.text: It does not work for many small zones where the queries are spread across multiple delegations.

chat.author: Shane Kerr
chat.text: I think this is completely orthogonal to this.

chat.author: Ray Bellis
chat.text: this Merkle tree is only in memory, not "in the DNS"

chat.author: Shane Kerr
chat.text: Rather, I think that MTL is completely orthogonal to this.

chat.author: Ondřej Surý
chat.text: Yes, the "Merkle tree" here is just "implementation" detail.

chat.author: Erik Nygren
chat.text: @ben: But if the queries don't all go to the same place then hit rate could be low and you'd need to resend the full signature+ladder much of the time.  (So might save on signing time but won't necessarily save bytes on the wire)
